questions.stem: Which nerve supplies buccinator?
options: Motor root of the trigeminal nerve
questions.explanation: Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve; it presses the cheek against the teeth to stop food escaping into the vestibule. The buccal nerve (V3) is purely sensory and supplies the skin and mucosa of the cheek; the similar names are often confused.
notes: It supplies only stylopharyngeus.
It carries sensation from the skin and mucosa of the cheek; it does not supply the muscle.
It supplies the muscles of mastication.
It supplies the tongue muscles.

questions.stem: A patient with an ischaemic stroke in the left hemisphere has a drooping right corner of the mouth and a flattened right nasolabial fold, but can wrinkle the forehead on both sides and close both eyes. What explains this finding?
options: The lesion is where the facial nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen.
Occipitofrontalis is supplied by cervical nerves.
The part of the facial nucleus supplying the upper face receives bilateral cortical fibres.
The lesion is in the course of the facial nerve within the pons.
The forehead muscles are supplied by the trigeminal nerve.
questions.explanation: In central (upper motor neuron) facial palsy only the lower half of the opposite face is affected, because the part of the facial nucleus controlling the forehead and orbicularis oculi receives corticobulbar fibres from both hemispheres. In peripheral (Bell's) palsy the whole face on the same side is involved.

questions.stem: A patient with Bell's palsy cannot close the right eye and complains of a dry eye. Which muscle closes the eye, and what is its nerve?
questions.explanation: Orbicularis oculi, which closes the eyelids, is supplied by the temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve. When it is paralysed the eye cannot close, the cornea dries and the efferent limb of the corneal reflex is lost. Levator, which raises the lid, is supplied by the oculomotor nerve.

questions.stem: Which muscle of mastication opens the mouth (protrudes and depresses the mandible)?
questions.explanation: Three of the four muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close the jaw. Lateral pterygoid initiates opening by pulling the condyle and disc forwards; gravity and the suprahyoid muscles complete the movement. All the muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).

questions.stem: Which is the main muscle that retracts the mandible?
questions.explanation: The fan-shaped fibres of temporalis run to the coronoid process. The anterior and middle fibres close the jaw; the almost horizontal posterior fibres pull the mandible backwards.

questions.stem: After a head injury a patient reports double vision, especially when going downstairs and reading; he holds his head tilted to the healthy side. Which muscle is paralysed?
questions.explanation: Superior oblique (trochlear nerve, IV) turns the eye down, especially when adducted, and intorts it. When paralysed there is vertical diplopia on looking down and in (going downstairs, reading); the patient tilts the head to the opposite side to compensate for the extorsion. The trochlear nerve is often injured in head trauma because of its long intracranial course.

questions.stem: In abducens nerve palsy, what is the resting position of the affected eye?
questions.explanation: The abducens nerve (VI) supplies only lateral rectus. In its palsy the unopposed medial rectus pulls the eye inwards (esotropia) and there is horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze. The 'down and out' position is characteristic of oculomotor palsy.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies levator palpebrae superioris?
questions.explanation: Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve; in III palsy there is complete ptosis. Its smooth muscle part, the superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle, is supplied by sympathetic fibres; the mild ptosis of Horner syndrome is due to this.

questions.stem: When the patient protrudes the tongue it deviates to the right. Which nerve and side is the lesion on?
questions.explanation: Genioglossus, which protrudes the tongue, pushes it forwards and towards the opposite side from each side. In a unilateral XII palsy the healthy side dominates and the tongue deviates towards the paralysed side (the side of the lesion). In chronic lesions there is wasting and fasciculation on that side.

questions.stem: Which of the following tongue muscles is NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve?
questions.explanation: All intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; the only exception is palatoglossus, regarded as a muscle of the soft palate, which receives a branch of the vagus (pharyngeal plexus).

questions.stem: Which muscle wrinkles the forehead and raises the eyebrows?
questions.explanation: The frontal belly of occipitofrontalis pulls the galea aponeurotica forwards, raises the eyebrows and forms horizontal lines on the forehead. The frontal belly is supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve, the occipital belly by the posterior auricular nerve.

questions.stem: Which muscle draws the corner of the mouth upwards and outwards when smiling?
questions.explanation: Zygomaticus major arises from the zygomatic bone and attaches to the modiolus at the corner of the mouth, producing the smiling expression. Depressor anguli oris pulls the corner of the mouth down, giving a sad expression.

questions.stem: Which muscle, contracting on one side, tilts the head towards the same shoulder and turns the face to the opposite side and upwards?
questions.explanation: SCM runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process. Contracting on one side it tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side; on both sides it flexes the head. In congenital torticollis the muscle becomes fibrosed and shortened. Its motor nerve is the accessory nerve.

questions.stem: Which nerve descends on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) descends beneath the prevertebral fascia on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior, running from lateral to medial, and enters the thorax through the thoracic inlet. The front of the scalene muscle is therefore an important surgical landmark.

questions.stem: Which structures pass through the gap between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius?
options: Common carotid artery and vagus nerve
Subclavian artery and the roots/trunks of the brachial plexus
Internal jugular vein and thoracic duct
questions.explanation: The subclavian artery and brachial plexus pass through the scalene gap; the subclavian vein passes in front of scalenus anterior. Hypertrophy or anomalies of the scalenes can cause thoracic outlet syndrome in this gap. The interscalene block is given here.

questions.stem: Which of the following suprahyoid muscle–nerve pairings is WRONG?
options: Digastric, anterior belly – nerve to mylohyoid
questions.explanation: Geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibres, which travel with the hypoglossal nerve. The two bellies of digastric have different nerves (V3 and VII) because they develop from different pharyngeal arches.

questions.stem: What supplies most of the infrahyoid muscles?
questions.explanation: Sternohyoid, sternothyroid and omohyoid are supplied by the ansa cervicalis. Thyrohyoid receives C1 fibres travelling with the hypoglossal nerve. The superior root of the ansa (C1) runs with XII, the inferior root comes from C2–C3.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies platysma?
questions.explanation: Platysma is a thin muscle of facial expression lying in the superficial cervical fascia, supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. It tenses the skin of the neck and pulls the corner of the mouth down.

questions.stem: After a lymph node biopsy from the posterior triangle of the neck, a patient's shoulder droops and he has difficulty raising the arm above 90° and shrugging. Which nerve and muscle are injured?
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve runs superficially in the posterior triangle and is easily injured in biopsies. The upper fibres of trapezius elevate the scapula and, with serratus anterior, rotate it upwards; when paralysed the shoulder droops and abduction above 90° becomes difficult.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies latissimus dorsi?
questions.explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8) arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. Latissimus dorsi extends, adducts and internally rotates the arm; it is powerful in climbing and swimming. It is used as a flap in reconstructive surgery.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the rhomboids?
questions.explanation: The dorsal scapular nerve arises directly from the C5 root, pierces scalenus medius and supplies levator scapulae and the rhomboids. The rhomboids pull the scapula backwards and upwards towards the spine.

questions.stem: Which nerves supply the deep (intrinsic) back muscles such as erector spinae?
options: Anterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
questions.explanation: The true back muscles (erector spinae, transversospinal and suboccipital muscles) are epaxial in origin and are supplied segmentally by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves. The superficial back muscles (trapezius, latissimus, rhomboids) belong to the limb and receive nerves derived from anterior rami.

questions.stem: Which artery runs in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, over the posterior arch of the atlas?
questions.explanation: The suboccipital triangle is bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior and inferior. In its floor, in the groove on the posterior arch of the atlas, lie the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1). The greater occipital nerve passes over the triangle.

questions.stem: Which structures bound the inferior lumbar triangle (Petit's triangle)?
options: Inguinal ligament, rectus abdominis and inferior epigastric artery
Quadratus lumborum, psoas major and diaphragm
Trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula
Erector spinae, 12th rib and internal oblique
Latissimus dorsi, external oblique and the iliac crest
questions.explanation: Petit's triangle lies between latissimus dorsi (posteromedially), external oblique (anterolaterally) and the iliac crest (base); its floor is formed by the internal oblique. Rare lumbar hernias can develop here. Trapezius, latissimus and the scapular border bound the triangle of auscultation.

questions.stem: After mastectomy and axillary dissection, when the patient stretches the arms forwards and pushes against a wall, the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall (winged scapula). Which nerve is injured?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) descends on the outer surface of serratus anterior along the medial wall of the axilla and is easily injured in axillary surgery. Serratus anterior presses the scapula against the chest wall and protracts it; when paralysed the scapula wings and the arm cannot be raised above 90°.

questions.stem: What is the nerve supply of pectoralis major?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis major is supplied by the lateral (C5–C7) and medial (C8–T1) pectoral nerves. It adducts and internally rotates the arm; its clavicular head flexes and its sternocostal head extends.

questions.stem: Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts?
questions.explanation: The axillary artery runs from the outer border of the 1st rib to the lower border of teres major; the part above pectoralis minor is the 1st part, behind it the 2nd and below it the 3rd. Pectoralis minor also divides the levels of the axillary lymph nodes.

questions.stem: Between which muscle layers do the intercostal vein, artery and nerve run?
options: Between the skin and the external intercostal
Between the external and internal intercostals
Between serratus anterior and the external intercostal
Between the internal intercostal and the innermost intercostal
Between the innermost intercostal and the parietal pleura
questions.explanation: The neurovascular bundle lies in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib, between the internal and innermost intercostals; from above down the order is vein, artery, nerve (VAN).

questions.stem: Which structures pass through the aortic hiatus?
options: Aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein
Inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve
Oesophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks
Aorta, vagus nerve and sympathetic trunk
questions.explanation: The three large openings of the diaphragm: caval opening (T8) – IVC and branches of the right phrenic nerve; oesophageal hiatus (T10) – oesophagus and vagal trunks; aortic hiatus (T12) – aorta, thoracic duct and usually the azygos vein. The aortic hiatus actually lies behind the diaphragm, between the crura.

questions.stem: After a traffic accident, a patient with a ruptured spleen complains of pain at the tip of the left shoulder (Kehr's sign). Which nerve carries this referred pain?
questions.explanation: Sensation from the central diaphragm and the peritoneum beneath it is carried by the phrenic nerve to segments C3–C5. The skin of the shoulder is also from the C4 dermatome; when blood under the diaphragm irritates the peritoneum, pain is referred to the shoulder tip.

questions.stem: Which of the following about the diaphragm is FALSE?
options: When it contracts its domes descend and the thoracic cavity enlarges.
An important part of its motor supply comes from the lower intercostal nerves.
The medial arcuate ligament passes over psoas major.
The right dome is higher than the left because of the liver.
The right crus encircles the oesophageal hiatus.
questions.explanation: The diaphragm's only motor nerve is the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). The lower intercostal nerves carry only sensation from its periphery. The right crus is larger, and most of the fibres encircling the oesophageal hiatus come from it.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Below the arcuate line, which statement about the rectus sheath is true?
options: The sheath has no anterior wall.
The internal oblique aponeurosis splits to enclose the muscle.
Its posterior wall is formed by quadratus lumborum.
The aponeuroses of the three flat muscles pass in front of the muscle; the posterior wall is formed only by the transversalis fascia.
The transversus abdominis aponeurosis passes behind the muscle.
questions.explanation: At about the midpoint between the umbilicus and symphysis (arcuate line) the posterior sheath ends. Below this level all the aponeuroses pass in front; rectus is covered behind only by the transversalis fascia and peritoneum. The inferior epigastric artery enters the sheath just below this line.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: At inguinal hernia surgery the sac is seen to enter the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and descend within the spermatic cord to the scrotum. Which hernia is this?
questions.explanation: An indirect hernia enters through the deep ring (lateral to the epigastric vessels), follows the canal and may descend to the scrotum; it is usually due to a patent processus vaginalis (congenital). A direct hernia emerges medial to the epigastric vessels through Hesselbach's triangle, pushing the posterior wall of the canal forwards.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: What are the boundaries of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle?
options: Superior epigastric artery, linea alba and lacunar ligament
Latissimus dorsi, external oblique and iliac crest
Inguinal ligament, sartorius and adductor longus
Inferior epigastric artery, lateral border of rectus abdominis and the inguinal ligament
Spermatic cord, inguinal ligament and linea semilunaris
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle is a weak area on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall through which direct inguinal hernias emerge. Laterally lies the inferior epigastric artery, medially the lateral border of rectus, and below the inguinal ligament.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: From which muscle does the cremaster arise, and which nerve supplies it?
options: Internal oblique – genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
questions.explanation: The cremaster fibres separate from the lower border of the internal oblique and wrap the spermatic cord. Elevation of the testis when the inner thigh is touched (cremasteric reflex) is mediated by the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2).

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Which muscles form the falx inguinalis (conjoint tendon)?
questions.explanation: The lower aponeurotic fibres of the internal oblique and transversus unite and attach to the pecten pubis, reinforcing the medial posterior wall of the inguinal canal. This is important in preventing direct hernias.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: The inguinal ligament is the rolled-under lower border of which structure?
options: Muscle fibres of the internal oblique
questions.explanation: The aponeurosis of the external oblique folds inwards between the ASIS and the pubic tubercle to form the inguinal ligament. The triangular opening in the same aponeurosis is the superficial inguinal ring.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Which muscle contributes importantly to faecal continence by maintaining the anorectal angle?
questions.explanation: Puborectalis, part of levator ani, forms a U-shaped sling behind the rectum and pulls the anorectal junction forwards, creating an angle of about 90°. In defecation it relaxes and straightens the angle.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Which is one of the main functions of quadratus lumborum?
options: To rotate the trunk to the opposite side
To fix the 12th rib during deep inspiration
questions.explanation: Quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest to the 12th rib and the lumbar transverse processes. By holding the 12th rib down it helps the diaphragm contract effectively; acting on one side it bends the trunk sideways.

questions.stem: Which muscle initiates the first 15° of abduction of the arm?
questions.explanation: Supraspinatus initiates abduction while pressing the humeral head into the glenoid cavity. Between 15° and 90° deltoid dominates; above 90° the scapula must rotate upwards through trapezius and serratus anterior.

questions.stem: Which rotator cuff muscles rotate the arm externally?
questions.explanation: Infraspinatus (suprascapular nerve) and teres minor (axillary nerve) attach to the posterior facets of the greater tubercle and are the main external rotators of the arm. Subscapularis, teres major, latissimus and pectoralis major rotate internally.

questions.stem: Which structures pass through the quadrangular space?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
questions.explanation: The quadrangular space is bounded by teres minor (above), teres major (below), the long head of triceps (medially) and the surgical neck of the humerus (laterally). The circumflex scapular artery passes through the triangular space, and the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery through the triangular interval.

questions.stem: Which muscles rotate the scapula upwards for abduction of the arm above 90° (elevation)?
options: Trapezius (upper and lower fibres) and serratus anterior
questions.explanation: Upward rotation of the scapula turns the glenoid fossa upwards. The upper and lower fibres of trapezius and the lower fibres of serratus anterior form a force couple. The rhomboids, levator scapulae and pectoralis minor rotate the scapula downwards.

questions.stem: A patient with shoulder pain is asked to place the back of the hand on the lower back and lift the hand away; he cannot (positive lift-off test). Tear of which muscle is suspected?
questions.explanation: In the lift-off test the arm is internally rotated, and lifting the hand off the back requires further internal rotation; this is the function of subscapularis. Supraspinatus is assessed with the 'empty can' (Jobe) test, infraspinatus with resisted external rotation.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies teres major?
questions.explanation: Teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve from the posterior cord; with latissimus dorsi it adducts, internally rotates and extends the arm. It is not part of the rotator cuff. Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve.

questions.stem: What is the main function of deltoid?
options: To abduct the arm between 15° and 90°
questions.explanation: The middle fibres of deltoid are a powerful abductor; the anterior fibres flex and internally rotate, the posterior fibres extend and externally rotate. The muscle is supplied by the axillary nerve, and for intramuscular injection the area about 3–5 cm below the acromion is used.

questions.stem: With the elbow flexed, which is the most powerful supinator of the forearm?
questions.explanation: Because biceps attaches to the radial tuberosity, it supinates very powerfully with the elbow at 90° (the screwdriver movement). With the elbow straight, supination is done mainly by supinator.

questions.stem: Which nerve pierces coracobrachialis?
questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve arises from the lateral cord, pierces coracobrachialis, runs between biceps and brachialis and ends in the forearm as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

questions.stem: Which is the main (most powerful) flexor of the elbow joint?
questions.explanation: Brachialis is the 'workhorse' flexor of the elbow in every forearm position; because it attaches to the ulna it is unaffected by forearm rotation. It is supplied mostly by the musculocutaneous nerve, with a small lateral part supplied by the radial nerve.

questions.stem: Which spinal segment does the triceps tendon reflex chiefly assess?
questions.explanation: The biceps reflex assesses C5–C6 (especially C5), the brachioradialis reflex C6 and the triceps reflex C7 (C6–C8). In a C6–C7 disc herniation (C7 root) the triceps reflex is reduced.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man lifting something heavy feels a 'snap' at the front of the shoulder; on bending the elbow a prominent mass forms in the lower front of the arm (Popeye sign). Which structure has torn?
options: Tendon of the long head of biceps brachii
questions.explanation: The tendon of the long head of biceps can tear from friction and degeneration in the intertubercular sulcus; the muscle belly slides down and forms a mass. Because the short head and brachialis are intact, elbow flexion is not markedly impaired.

questions.stem: What is the order of structures in the cubital fossa from lateral to medial?
options: Brachial artery – biceps tendon – median nerve
Radial nerve – median nerve – brachial artery
Biceps tendon – median nerve – brachial artery
Biceps tendon – brachial artery – median nerve
Median nerve – brachial artery – biceps tendon
questions.explanation: In the cubital fossa, from lateral to medial, lie the biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve. The radial nerve lies deeper and more laterally under brachioradialis. When measuring blood pressure the stethoscope is placed medial to the biceps tendon.

questions.stem: Between the two heads of which muscle does the median nerve usually pass as it enters the forearm?
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres; compression here causes pronator syndrome. The ulnar nerve passes between the two heads of FCU, and the deep branch of the radial nerve through supinator.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the part of flexor digitorum profundus going to the 4th and 5th fingers?
options: Main trunk of the median nerve
questions.explanation: FDP has a dual supply: its lateral half to the 2nd and 3rd fingers is supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, its medial half to the 4th and 5th fingers by the ulnar nerve.

questions.stem: After a forearm fracture the patient cannot make an 'OK' sign by touching the tips of the thumb and index finger; because he cannot flex the fingertips, the pulps touch instead of the nail tips. There is no sensory loss. Which nerve is injured?
options: Recurrent branch of the median nerve
Superficial branch of the radial nerve
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch of the median nerve: it supplies FPL, the lateral half of FDP and pronator quadratus. When paralysed, flexion of the distal phalanges of the thumb and index finger is lost; as it has no sensory branch, there is no sensory loss.

questions.stem: Which muscle, although in the forearm and supplied by the radial nerve, flexes the elbow in the mid-prone position?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is a muscle of the extensor (posterior) compartment and is supplied by the radial nerve; but because it passes in front of the elbow joint it flexes the elbow, especially with the forearm in the mid-position.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: Nine tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) pass through the carpal tunnel with the median nerve. The palmaris longus tendon passes in front of the flexor retinaculum to join the palmar aponeurosis; it is absent in about 15% of people and is used as a tendon graft.

questions.stem: After a radial head fracture the patient cannot extend the fingers at the MCP joints. He can lift the wrist, but it deviates radially. There is no sensory loss in the hand. Which nerve is injured?
options: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Main trunk of the radial nerve (in the radial groove)
Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve)
questions.explanation: The deep branch passes through supinator (arcade of Frohse) to become the posterior interosseous nerve and supplies the finger extensors and ECU. ECRL is spared because its branch arises before the division; wrist extension deviates radially. As the sensory superficial branch is unaffected, there is no sensory loss.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old tennis player has tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and pain on resisted wrist extension. The origin tendon of which muscle is most often affected?
questions.explanation: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) is an overuse degeneration of the common extensor origin, most often the ECRB tendon. Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) involves the common flexor–pronator origin.

questions.stem: Which tendon forms the ulnar (medial) border of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The radial border of the snuffbox is formed by the APL and EPB tendons, the ulnar border by the EPL tendon. Its floor contains the scaphoid and trapezium, and the radial artery runs within it. The EPL tendon changes direction around the dorsal tubercle of the radius (Lister's).

questions.stem: A new mother complains of pain on the radial side of the wrist when holding her baby. Pain increases when the thumb is held in the palm and the wrist is deviated ulnarly (Finkelstein test). Which tendons are affected?
options: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Extensor digitorum and extensor digiti minimi
Flexor pollicis longus and flexor carpi radialis
Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
questions.explanation: De Quervain's tenosynovitis is inflammation of the sheath of the APL and EPB tendons, which run together in the first dorsal compartment over the radial styloid.

questions.stem: What are the nerve supply and action of flexor carpi ulnaris?
options: Median nerve – pronation of the forearm
Median nerve – flexion and abduction of the wrist
Ulnar nerve – flexion and adduction (ulnar deviation) of the wrist
Radial nerve – adduction of the wrist
Ulnar nerve – extension of the wrist
questions.explanation: FCU is the only superficial forearm flexor supplied by the ulnar nerve; it attaches through the pisiform to the hamate and 5th metacarpal. FCR is supplied by the median nerve and deviates the wrist radially.

questions.stem: Which thumb muscle is supplied by the ulnar nerve?
options: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
questions.explanation: The thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, superficial head of FPB) are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Adductor pollicis and the deep head of FPB receive the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

questions.stem: What is the action of the lumbricals in the hand?
options: To flex only the distal phalanges
To flex the MCP joints and extend the interphalangeal joints
To extend the MCP joints and flex the interphalangeal joints
questions.explanation: The lumbricals arise from the FDP tendons and attach to the radial side of the extensor hood. They therefore flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints (the writing position). The 1st and 2nd lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve, the 3rd and 4th by the ulnar nerve.

questions.stem: The patient is asked to grip a sheet of paper firmly between thumb and index finger; when the paper is pulled he tries to hold it by flexing the tip joint of the thumb (Froment's sign). Which muscle is weak and which nerve is damaged?
options: Flexor pollicis longus – anterior interosseous nerve
questions.explanation: When adductor pollicis is weak the patient uses FPL, supplied by the median nerve, to hold the paper, and the IP joint of the thumb flexes. This is a classic sign of ulnar nerve damage.

questions.stem: In carpal tunnel syndrome, why is sensation over the lateral half of the palm usually preserved?
options: The palm is supplied by the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
The palmar skin is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.
The palmar skin is supplied only by the ulnar nerve.
The palmar branch of the median nerve arises before the carpal tunnel and passes in front of the retinaculum.
questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch arises a few centimetres above the wrist and does not use the tunnel. So in carpal tunnel syndrome sensory loss is limited to the fingers (palmar surface of the lateral 3½ digits); if the palm is involved, the lesion is more proximal.

questions.stem: Which statement about the palmar and dorsal interossei is true?
options: They are all supplied by the median nerve.
The palmar interossei adduct the fingers, the dorsal interossei abduct them.
The dorsal interossei adduct the fingers.
The axis is the 4th finger, that of the middle finger.
questions.explanation: 'PAD–DAB': Palmar ADduct, Dorsal ABduct. Movements are defined relative to the axis of the middle finger. All the interossei are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve; like the lumbricals they flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints.

questions.stem: Why is the claw-hand deformity milder in a patient whose ulnar nerve is injured at the elbow than in one injured at the wrist?
options: At the elbow all the lumbricals are spared.
At the elbow the ulnar part of FDP is also paralysed, so IP flexion of the 4th–5th fingers is reduced.
At the elbow the interossei are spared.
At the wrist the median nerve is also affected.
At the wrist the extensors are paralysed.
questions.explanation: In a claw hand the MCP joints are hyperextended and the IP joints flexed; the flexion is produced by FDP. In a high (elbow) lesion the ulnar half of FDP is also paralysed, so clawing is less. This is known as the 'ulnar paradox'.

questions.stem: After hip surgery the patient can walk on level ground but has difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. Which muscle and nerve are affected?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus is the powerful extensor of the hip and comes into play especially when moving from flexion to extension (rising from a chair, climbing stairs, running). Its contribution to normal walking is small.

questions.stem: While the patient stands on the right leg, the left side of the pelvis drops (positive Trendelenburg sign). Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: When standing on one leg, gluteus medius and minimus of that side keep the pelvis level. In right superior gluteal nerve palsy, standing on the right leg lets the unsupported left pelvis drop. When walking the patient compensates by leaning the trunk towards the paralysed side.

questions.stem: Which is the safe area for intramuscular injection into the gluteal region, and why?
options: Upper inner quadrant; because it is away from the superior gluteal nerve
Upper outer quadrant; because it is away from the sciatic nerve
Lower outer quadrant; because it is away from the large vessels
Exact centre; because the muscle layer is thinnest
Lower inner quadrant; because the muscle mass is thickest
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve emerges in the lower inner part of the gluteal region, below piriformis, and descends between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity. The upper outer quadrant (or ventrogluteal site) is therefore preferred.

questions.stem: Which nerve passes through the part of the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis (suprapiriform)?
questions.explanation: Only the superior gluteal nerve and the superior gluteal artery and vein pass through the suprapiriform opening. Through the infrapiriform opening pass the inferior gluteal nerve, sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, pudendal nerve, internal pudendal artery and the nerves to the short rotators.

questions.stem: In a patient with right lower quadrant pain, pain increases when he lies on his left side and the right hip is passively extended. On which muscle does this suggest the inflamed appendix lies?
questions.explanation: Psoas sign: an inflamed retrocaecal appendix touches the fascia of psoas; extending the hip stretches the muscle and increases the pain. The obturator sign is pain on flexion and internal rotation of the hip in pelvic appendicitis.

questions.stem: What are the nerve supply and action of tensor fasciae latae?
options: Inferior gluteal nerve – extends the hip
Superior gluteal nerve – tenses the iliotibial tract and flexes and abducts the hip
questions.explanation: TFL is supplied by the same nerve as gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve). Through the iliotibial tract it also stabilises the outer side of the knee; excessive tightness leads to iliotibial band syndrome.

questions.stem: Which is the longest muscle in the body, also known as the 'tailor's muscle'?
questions.explanation: Sartorius arises from the ASIS, crosses the thigh and attaches to the medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus). It flexes, abducts and externally rotates the hip and flexes the knee (cross-legged sitting). It is supplied by the femoral nerve and forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.

questions.stem: Which head of quadriceps femoris both flexes the hip and extends the knee?
questions.explanation: Because rectus femoris arises from the AIIS and the upper rim of the acetabulum it also crosses the hip joint; the three vasti arise only from the femur and only extend the knee. All of quadriceps is supplied by the femoral nerve.

questions.stem: With which nerve is the 'hamstring part' of the doubly innervated adductor magnus supplied?
options: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve
Fibular part of the sciatic nerve
Posterior branch of the obturator nerve
questions.explanation: The adductor part of adductor magnus is supplied by the obturator nerve, the hamstring part arising from the ischial tuberosity by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. The opening between the two parts is the adductor hiatus.

questions.stem: Which structures pass through the adductor hiatus to reach the popliteal fossa?
options: Anterior branch of the obturator nerve
questions.explanation: After following the adductor canal, the femoral artery and vein pass through the opening in adductor magnus and become the popliteal artery and vein. The saphenous nerve leaves the canal and turns to the medial side of the knee without entering the hiatus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT found in the adductor (Hunter's) canal?
questions.explanation: The adductor canal lies under sartorius, between vastus medialis and the adductors; the femoral artery and vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis pass through it. The great saphenous vein is a superficial vein running in the superficial fascia.

questions.stem: Which muscle of the hamstring group is supplied by the common fibular nerve?
questions.explanation: Most hamstring muscles receive the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. The short head of biceps femoris arises from the femur (linea aspera), is not a true hamstring and is supplied by the fibular part.

questions.stem: To which muscles do the tendons forming the pes anserinus belong?
questions.explanation: The three tendons join on the upper medial surface of the tibia in a goose-foot shape and are supplied by three different nerves: sartorius (femoral nerve), gracilis (obturator nerve), semitendinosus (sciatic nerve–tibial part). Inflammation of the bursa beneath them is pes anserinus bursitis.

questions.stem: Which thigh muscle may be supplied by both the femoral nerve and the obturator nerve?
questions.explanation: Pectineus is supplied mainly by the femoral nerve and often also by the obturator (or accessory obturator) nerve; it is therefore regarded as a transitional muscle between the anterior and medial compartments.

questions.stem: Which muscle forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded above by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the medial border of sartorius and medially by the medial border of adductor longus. Its floor is formed by iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus; it contains, from lateral to medial, the femoral nerve, artery, vein and lymphatics.

questions.stem: What are the nerve supply and action of tibialis anterior?
options: Deep fibular nerve – everts the foot
Deep fibular nerve – dorsiflexes and inverts the foot
Superficial fibular nerve – everts the foot
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior is the strongest dorsiflexor in the anterior compartment of the leg and raises the medial border of the foot. The anterior compartment muscles are supplied by the deep fibular nerve.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis?
questions.explanation: The lateral compartment muscles (fibularis longus and brevis) are supplied by the superficial fibular nerve and are the main evertors of the foot. The nerve then pierces the fascia and supplies most of the skin of the dorsum of the foot.

questions.stem: After a tight cast, a patient develops severe pain at the front of the leg; passive flexion of the big toe increases the pain, and sensation is lost in a small area between the 1st and 2nd toes. Which compartment and nerve are affected?
questions.explanation: In anterior compartment syndrome the muscles within (tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL) hurt on passive stretch. The nerve of this compartment is the deep fibular nerve, which supplies only the first web space in the skin. Early fasciotomy is needed.

questions.stem: Which spinal segment does the ankle (Achilles) reflex mainly assess?
questions.explanation: The ankle reflex tests segment S1 (S1–S2) through triceps surae and the tibial nerve. The patellar reflex assesses L4 (L3–L4). L5 has no reliable reflex.

questions.stem: Which muscle is called the 'peripheral heart' because of its contribution to venous return?
questions.explanation: Soleus contains large venous sinuses; when it contracts it squeezes the deep veins and pumps blood upwards (muscle pump). Prolonged immobility disables this pump and raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: What is the order of structures behind the medial malleolus from front to back?
options: Flexor digitorum longus, tibialis posterior, tibial nerve, posterior tibial artery, flexor hallucis longus
Tibial nerve, posterior tibial artery, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus
Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery/vein, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus
Flexor hallucis longus, tibial nerve, posterior tibial artery, flexor digitorum longus, tibialis posterior
Tibialis posterior, posterior tibial artery, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus, tibial nerve
questions.explanation: In the tarsal tunnel (under the flexor retinaculum) the order from front to back is: tibialis posterior, FDL, artery and veins, tibial nerve, FHL. Compression of the tibial nerve here is tarsal tunnel syndrome. The posterior tibial pulse is felt between the medial malleolus and the heel.

questions.stem: A basketball player jumping feels as if kicked in the back of the heel; lying prone, squeezing the calf does not plantarflex the foot (positive Thompson test). Which structure is injured?
questions.explanation: The Achilles tendon is the common tendon of gastrocnemius and soleus. In a complete rupture squeezing the calf does not move the foot. The slender plantaris tendon may remain intact but cannot produce the movement on its own.

questions.stem: Which leg muscle, absent in some people, has a tendon that can be used as a tendon graft?
questions.explanation: Plantaris has a small belly and one of the longest tendons in the body; it descends between gastrocnemius and soleus to attach to the calcaneus. Because it has little functional importance, it can be harvested as a graft.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the muscles of the dorsum of the foot (extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis)?
questions.explanation: The short extensors, the only muscle group on the dorsum of the foot, are supplied by the lateral branch of the deep fibular nerve. All the muscles of the sole come from the medial and lateral plantar branches of the tibial nerve.

questions.stem: Which of the following plantar muscles is supplied by the medial plantar nerve?
questions.explanation: The medial plantar nerve resembles the median nerve in the hand: it supplies abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and the 1st lumbrical. All the other plantar muscles are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve (the counterpart of the ulnar nerve in the hand).

questions.stem: Which muscle, supplied by the trochlear nerve, turns the eyeball down and out?
questions.explanation: The superior oblique tendon passes through the trochlea, changes direction and attaches to the posterior superolateral quadrant of the eyeball; it intorts the eye and turns it down and out. The trochlear nerve (IV) supplies only this muscle. In clinical testing, looking down with the eye adducted assesses this muscle.
notes: It turns the eye up and in; supplied by the oculomotor nerve.
It turns the eye down and in; supplied by the oculomotor nerve.
It only abducts; supplied by the abducens nerve.
It turns the eye up and out; supplied by the oculomotor nerve.

questions.stem: Which muscle produces upward gaze when the eye is looking inwards (adducted)?
questions.explanation: In clinical examination the obliques are tested with the eye adducted and the recti with it abducted: looking up while looking in tests inferior oblique, looking up while looking out tests superior rectus. Inferior oblique is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve.
notes: It is the muscle of upward gaze when looking out.
It raises the eyelid; it does not move the eyeball.
It is the muscle of downward gaze when looking in.
It only adducts.

questions.stem: A patient presenting with an aneurysm has complete drooping of the right eyelid; when the lid is lifted the right eye looks down and out and the pupil is dilated and unreactive to light. Which nerve is affected?
questions.explanation: In oculomotor palsy levator palpebrae (complete ptosis), superior, inferior and medial recti and inferior oblique are paralysed; the eye turns down and out under the unopposed lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV). The parasympathetic fibres on the surface of the nerve are affected early by compression, so the pupil dilates. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm is the classic cause.
notes: In Horner syndrome the ptosis is mild and the pupil is small.
When paralysed the eye turns in; there is no ptosis.
It closes the eye; it does not raise the lid.
When paralysed the eye cannot look down in adduction; there is no ptosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following extra-ocular muscles does NOT arise from the common tendinous ring?
questions.explanation: The four recti arise from the common tendinous ring surrounding the optic canal and the medial part of the superior orbital fissure. Inferior oblique arises from the anteromedial floor of the orbit (orbital surface of the maxilla) and is the only extra-ocular muscle that does not originate at the back of the orbit.

questions.stem: Which smooth muscle raises the upper eyelid and is supplied by sympathetic fibres?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle fibres separating from the underside of levator palpebrae superioris attach to the tarsal plate and are supplied by the sympathetic system. In Horner syndrome paralysis of this muscle causes a mild ptosis of 1–2 mm; complete ptosis suggests oculomotor palsy.
notes: It is striated muscle supplied by the oculomotor nerve.
It draws the eyebrows together; supplied by the facial nerve.
It wrinkles the forehead; supplied by the facial nerve.
It closes the eyelid; supplied by the facial nerve.

questions.stem: Where does the upper head of lateral pterygoid attach?
options: Pterygoid tuberosity on the inner surface of the angle of the mandible
Articular disc and capsule of the temporomandibular joint
Outer surface of the ramus of the mandible
questions.explanation: The upper head of lateral pterygoid attaches to the articular disc and capsule, the lower head to the pterygoid fovea on the neck of the mandible. On opening the mouth it pulls the condyle and disc forwards together towards the articular tubercle. Temporalis attaches to the coronoid process, medial pterygoid to the inner surface of the angle and masseter to its outer surface.
notes: This is the insertion of medial pterygoid.
This is the insertion of temporalis.
This is the origin of mylohyoid.
This is the insertion of masseter.

questions.stem: Which muscle of mastication attaches to the inner surface of the angle of the mandible?
questions.explanation: Medial pterygoid arises from the inner surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and attaches to the inner surface of the angle of the mandible (pterygoid tuberosity). With masseter it forms a 'sling' around the mandible from inside and outside and closes the jaw.

questions.stem: What is the insertion of temporalis?
options: Coronoid process of the mandible and anterior border of the ramus
questions.explanation: Temporalis arises fan-like from the whole temporal fossa, passes under the zygomatic arch and attaches to the coronoid process. Its anterior fibres close the jaw and its posterior horizontal fibres retract the mandible; it is supplied by the deep temporal branches of the mandibular nerve.

questions.stem: Which is the main muscle that protrudes the tongue?
questions.explanation: Genioglossus arises from the superior mental spine; its posterior fibres pull the root of the tongue forwards and protrude the tongue. In unilateral hypoglossal palsy the healthy genioglossus pushes the tongue across, so it deviates to the side of the lesion. Hyoglossus pulls the tongue down, styloglossus back and up.
notes: It pulls the tongue up and back.
It raises the root of the tongue; supplied by the vagus nerve.
It forms the floor of the mouth; it is not a tongue muscle.
It pulls the tongue down and back.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT pass on the superficial (outer) surface of hyoglossus?
options: Vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve
questions.explanation: Hyoglossus is an important landmark of the submandibular region: the hypoglossal nerve with its accompanying vein, the lingual nerve and the submandibular duct run on its surface, while the lingual artery passes deep (medial) to it. In surgery the lingual artery is therefore sought at the posterior border of the muscle.

questions.stem: Where does the intermediate tendon joining the two bellies of digastric attach?
options: To the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
To the digastric fossa of the mandible
To the mastoid notch of the mastoid process
By a fibrous loop to the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone
questions.explanation: The anterior belly arises from the digastric fossa and the posterior belly from the mastoid notch; the intermediate tendon is bound to the hyoid by a fibrous sling and passes between the split tendon of stylohyoid. The anterior belly is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid (V3), the posterior belly by the facial nerve.
notes: This is the attachment of sternothyroid and thyrohyoid.
This is the origin of the anterior belly.
This is the origin of stylohyoid and styloglossus.
This is the origin of the posterior belly.

questions.stem: Which muscle forms the floor of the mouth (oral diaphragm)?
questions.explanation: The two mylohyoid muscles arise from the mylohyoid lines of the mandible and meet at the midline raphe and the body of the hyoid, forming the floor of the mouth. The superficial and deep parts of the submandibular gland curve around the posterior border of this muscle.

questions.stem: What holds the intermediate tendon of omohyoid in place?
options: The greater horn of the hyoid bone
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
The back of the manubrium of the sternum
A fascial sling attached to the clavicle and 1st rib
questions.explanation: The inferior belly of omohyoid arises from the upper border of the scapula (near the suprascapular notch), the superior belly from the body of the hyoid. The two bellies meet in front of the internal jugular vein at the intermediate tendon, which is held to the clavicle and 1st rib by a sling of deep cervical fascia.

questions.stem: Into which two smaller triangles does the inferior belly of omohyoid divide the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle (between SCM, trapezius and clavicle) is divided by the inferior belly of omohyoid into the occipital triangle above and the omoclavicular (supraclavicular) triangle below. The accessory nerve crosses the occipital triangle; the third part of the subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus lie in the omoclavicular triangle.

questions.stem: Which muscles bound the carotid triangle?
options: The two bellies of digastric and the mandible
Anterior belly of digastric, hyoid bone and the midline of the neck
Sternocleidomastoid, superior belly of omohyoid and the midline of the neck
Sternocleidomastoid, superior belly of omohyoid and posterior belly of digastric
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle contains the bifurcation of the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, the vagus nerve and the hypoglossal nerve. The other options are, respectively, the boundaries of the submandibular, submental, posterior and muscular triangles.

questions.stem: Where do the two heads of sternocleidomastoid arise?
options: Manubrium of the sternum and 1st costal cartilage
Front of the manubrium of the sternum and medial 1/3 of the clavicle
Lateral 1/3 of the clavicle and acromion
Mastoid process and superior nuchal line
Body of the sternum and xiphoid process
questions.explanation: The sternal head arises from the front of the manubrium and the clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle; the muscle attaches to the mastoid process and lateral half of the superior nuchal line. The small triangular hollow between the two heads (lesser supraclavicular fossa) lies over the internal jugular vein.

questions.stem: What is the insertion of scalenus anterior?
options: Behind the groove for the subclavian artery on the 1st rib
questions.explanation: Scalenus anterior arises from the anterior tubercles of the C3–C6 transverse processes and attaches to the scalene tubercle of the 1st rib. The subclavian vein passes in front of this tubercle and the subclavian artery in the groove behind it. Scalenus medius attaches to the 1st rib behind the groove, scalenus posterior to the 2nd rib.
notes: This is the insertion of subclavius.
Scalenus anterior never attaches to C7.
This is the insertion of scalenus medius.
This is the insertion of scalenus posterior.

questions.stem: Which laryngeal muscle tenses the vocal folds and is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve?
questions.explanation: Cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage forwards and downwards, lengthening and tensing the vocal folds; it is important for high notes. It is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle on the outer surface of the larynx and is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; all the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: Which is the only laryngeal muscle that opens the rima glottidis (abducts the vocal folds)?
questions.explanation: Posterior cricoarytenoid pulls the muscular processes of the arytenoids backwards, rotating the vocal processes outwards and opening the glottis. In bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralysis of these muscles leaves the vocal folds in the midline, with stridor and respiratory distress.
notes: It tenses the vocal folds; it does not open them.
It relaxes the vocal folds.
It brings the vocal folds together.
It draws the arytenoids together and closes the posterior glottis.

questions.stem: After total thyroidectomy a patient becomes hoarse. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal fold immobile in the paramedian position. Which nerve has been damaged?
options: Internal branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
Superior root of the ansa cervicalis
External branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid and lies close to the inferior thyroid artery. In unilateral injury the vocal fold stays in the paramedian position and the voice is hoarse. Injury to the external branch causes voice fatigue and difficulty with high notes; the internal branch is sensory.
notes: It carries sensation from the mucosa above the glottis; it is not motor.
It supplies the infrahyoid muscles.
It supplies the tongue muscles.
It supplies only cricothyroid.

questions.stem: Which is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
questions.explanation: All the pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus; the only exception is stylopharyngeus, arising from the styloid process (glossopharyngeal nerve). It enters the pharynx between the superior and middle constrictors and raises the pharynx in swallowing.

questions.stem: Where is Killian's triangle, through which a Zenker diverticulum emerges?
options: Between the middle and inferior constrictors
Between the cricopharyngeal fibres and the longitudinal muscle layer of the oesophagus
Between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor
Between the superior and middle constrictors
Between stylopharyngeus and the superior constrictor
questions.explanation: Killian's triangle is the weak posterior area between the oblique thyropharyngeal fibres and the horizontal cricopharyngeal fibres (upper oesophageal sphincter) of the inferior constrictor. When the cricopharyngeal fibres fail to relax, the mucosa herniates backwards here. The area between cricopharyngeus and the oesophageal muscles is Laimer's triangle.

questions.stem: Which muscle, lying deep to trapezius at the back of the neck, turns the head to the same side?
questions.explanation: Splenius capitis arises from the nuchal ligament and upper thoracic spinous processes and attaches to the mastoid process and superior nuchal line; contracting on one side it turns the head to the same side. SCM turns the face to the opposite side; the two muscles work together in turning the head.
notes: It tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side.
It bends the neck to the same side; it does not turn the head.
It elevates the scapula.
It turns the face to the opposite side.

questions.stem: Which muscles bound the suboccipital triangle?
options: Longissimus capitis, rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis inferior
Rectus capitis posterior minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior
Rectus capitis posterior minor and major, and obliquus capitis inferior
Semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis and obliquus capitis superior
Rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior and obliquus capitis inferior
questions.explanation: The superomedial border of the triangle is rectus capitis posterior major, the superolateral border obliquus capitis superior and the inferior border obliquus capitis inferior. Its floor is the posterior arch of the atlas and posterior atlanto-occipital membrane; it contains the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve; its roof is covered by semispinalis capitis.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the suboccipital muscles?
options: Lesser occipital nerve (anterior ramus of C2)
Greater occipital nerve (posterior ramus of C2)
Third occipital nerve (posterior ramus of C3)
questions.explanation: The suboccipital nerve, the posterior ramus of C1, emerges between the vertebral artery and the posterior arch of the atlas and supplies all the muscles of the suboccipital triangle; it usually has no cutaneous branch. The greater occipital nerve emerges below obliquus capitis inferior and supplies the skin of the back of the neck and scalp.
notes: It carries sensation from the skin behind the ear.
It carries sensation from the back of the neck and scalp; it does not supply the suboccipital muscles.
It supplies trapezius and SCM.
It supplies the skin of the lower back of the neck.

questions.stem: Which muscle turns the head to the same side and forms the inferior border of the suboccipital triangle?
questions.explanation: Obliquus capitis inferior, running from the spine of the axis to the transverse process of the atlas, is the only suboccipital muscle that does not attach to the skull; it rotates the atlas and head on the axis to the same side.

questions.stem: Which structures bound the triangle of auscultation?
options: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula
Latissimus dorsi, external oblique and iliac crest
Quadratus lumborum, 12th rib and internal oblique
Teres major, teres minor and the long head of triceps
questions.explanation: In the triangle of auscultation the muscle layer is thin; when the patient leans forwards and folds the arms, the scapula moves laterally, the triangle widens and lung sounds are heard better. The other options are the inferior lumbar (Petit), superior lumbar (Grynfeltt), posterior cervical triangles and the scapular spaces.

questions.stem: Which is the most lateral column of erector spinae?
questions.explanation: From lateral to medial erector spinae consists of the iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns ('I Love Spaghetti'). Multifidus and semispinalis belong to the deeper transversospinal group. All are supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves.

questions.stem: Which transversospinal muscle is thickest in the lumbar region and plays an important role in segmental stabilisation?
questions.explanation: Multifidus extends from the sacrum to C2 and is thickest in the lumbar region; it binds each vertebra to the 2–4 below and stabilises the segments. Its wasting and fatty infiltration are common in chronic low back pain. Semispinalis is prominent in the thoracic–cervical region, rotatores in the thoracic region.

questions.stem: Where does rhomboid major insert?
options: Medial border of the scapula, from the root of the spine to the inferior angle
The small part of the medial border of the scapula at the level of the spine
Along the medial border of the anterior surface of the scapula
questions.explanation: Rhomboid major arises from the spinous processes of T2–T5 and inserts into the part of the medial border of the scapula below the spine; rhomboid minor runs from C7–T1 to the level of the root of the spine. Both are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and pull the scapula backwards and upwards.
notes: This is the insertion of pectoralis minor.
This is the insertion of rhomboid minor.
This is the insertion of levator scapulae.
This is the insertion of serratus anterior.

questions.stem: Where does levator scapulae arise?
options: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1–C4
Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3–C6
Superior nuchal line and nuchal ligament
questions.explanation: Levator scapulae arises from the upper cervical vertebrae and attaches to the superior angle and upper medial border of the scapula. It elevates the scapula and rotates it downwards; it is supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and branches of C3–C4.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an action of latissimus dorsi?
options: Pulling the trunk up with the arms fixed
questions.explanation: Latissimus dorsi attaches to the floor of the intertubercular sulcus; it extends, adducts and internally rotates the arm (the 'swimmer's muscle'). With the arms fixed (pull-up) it pulls the trunk upwards. External rotation is the job of infraspinatus and teres minor.

questions.stem: Where does serratus anterior insert?
options: Upper border of the spine of the scapula
Anterior (costal) surface of the medial border of the scapula
Posterior surface of the medial border of the scapula
questions.explanation: Serratus anterior arises by digitations from the upper 8–9 ribs and inserts into the anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula, its thickest fibres to the inferior angle. It holds the scapula against the chest wall and protracts it; its lower fibres rotate the scapula upwards, helping the arm rise above 90°.

questions.stem: Where does pectoralis minor arise and insert?
options: Arises from the clavicle and sternum, inserts into the crest of the greater tubercle
Arises from the 1st rib and its cartilage, inserts into the underside of the clavicle
Arises from ribs 2–5, inserts into the acromion
Arises from ribs 1–8, inserts into the medial border of the scapula
Arises from ribs 3–5, inserts into the coracoid process
questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor is the landmark dividing the axillary artery into three parts. The other options describe pectoralis major, subclavius and serratus anterior; no chest muscle attaches to the acromion.
notes: This describes pectoralis major.
This describes subclavius.
No chest muscle attaches to the acromion.
This describes serratus anterior.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT act as an accessory muscle of respiration in forced inspiration?
questions.explanation: In forced inspiration muscles that raise the rib cage assist: SCM, the scalenes, pectoralis minor (with the arm fixed) and serratus posterior superior. The anterior abdominal wall muscles raise intra-abdominal pressure and act in forced expiration and coughing.

questions.stem: What are the vertebral levels of the caval, oesophageal and aortic openings of the diaphragm, respectively?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon at T8, the oesophagus and vagal trunks through the muscle fibres of the right crus at T10, and the aorta behind the diaphragm (under the median arcuate ligament) at T12. Memory aid: 'I ate ten eggs at twelve' (IVC 8, oesophagus 10, aorta 12).

questions.stem: Which structures pass through the oesophageal hiatus?
options: Oesophagus, vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric artery and vein
Inferior vena cava and branches of the right phrenic nerve
Aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein
questions.explanation: The oesophageal opening lies at T10 between the muscle fibres of the right crus; with the oesophagus pass the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and the oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels. The ring formed by the muscle fibres acts like a physiological sphincter, and hiatus hernia develops here.
notes: It passes through the caval opening.
They pass behind or through the crura.
They pass through the aortic hiatus.
It passes through the sternocostal triangle (Larrey).

questions.stem: Which statement about the external intercostals is true?
options: Their fibres run vertically; they act only in coughing
Their fibres run downwards and forwards; they raise the ribs in inspiration
They extend as muscle in front as far as the sternum
Their fibres run downwards and backwards; they lower the ribs in expiration
The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs just deep to this muscle
questions.explanation: The external intercostals run downwards and forwards in the 'hands in pockets' direction and raise the ribs in inspiration; in front, between the cartilages, they become the external intercostal membrane. The internal intercostals run downwards and backwards. The neurovascular bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostals.
notes: There is no such muscle.
In front they become the external intercostal membrane.
This describes the internal intercostals.
The bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostals.

questions.stem: Where is transversus thoracis found?
options: It runs from the transverse processes of the vertebrae to the ribs below
It forms the deepest muscle layer of the anterior abdominal wall
It runs near the angles of the ribs, skipping one or two intercostal spaces
It lies at the root of the neck above the 1st rib
It runs from the back of the sternum to the inner surfaces of costal cartilages 2–6
questions.explanation: Transversus thoracis is a thin muscle on the inner surface of the anterior chest wall, behind the internal thoracic artery and vein; it is regarded as the thoracic continuation of transversus abdominis. Two of the other descriptions fit the subcostal muscles and the levatores costarum.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: What does the linea semilunaris indicate?
options: The lateral border of the rectus sheath
The medial end of the inguinal ligament
The midline separating the two recti
The lower limit of the posterior layer of the rectus sheath
questions.explanation: The linea semilunaris is the curved line along the lateral border of the rectus sheath where the aponeuroses of the flat muscles meet; the gallbladder projects onto it at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage. The lower limit of the posterior layer is the arcuate line, and the midline is the linea alba.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Where is a Spigelian hernia most often found?
options: Along the linea semilunaris, at the level of the arcuate line
In the linea alba above the umbilicus
questions.explanation: A Spigelian hernia develops through the weak point of the transversus abdominis aponeurosis at the edge of rectus (Spigelian fascia), mostly at the level of the arcuate line where the posterior rectus sheath ends. Because it lies beneath the external oblique aponeurosis, it can be hard to feel.
notes: This is the site of umbilical hernia.
This is the site of direct inguinal hernia.
This is the site of epigastric hernia.
This is the site of lumbar hernia.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Which is the deepest of the three flat muscles of the anterolateral abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: From superficial to deep: external oblique (downwards and forwards), internal oblique (upwards and forwards) and transversus abdominis (horizontal). Beneath transversus lie the transversalis fascia and peritoneum; its deep fibres act as a 'corset' raising intra-abdominal pressure.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Above the arcuate line, which structures form the posterior layer of the rectus sheath?
options: All the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles
The posterior lamina of the internal oblique aponeurosis and the transversus abdominis aponeurosis
The external and internal oblique aponeuroses
questions.explanation: Above the arcuate line the internal oblique aponeurosis splits: its anterior lamina joins the external oblique in the anterior sheath, its posterior lamina joins transversus in the posterior sheath. Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass in front; only the transversalis fascia remains behind rectus.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: What is the function of pyramidalis?
options: It is the main flexor of the trunk
questions.explanation: Pyramidalis is a small triangular muscle arising from the pubis and attaching to the linea alba; it lies within the rectus sheath, in front of rectus abdominis, and is absent in some people. It is supplied by the subcostal nerve (T12).

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Where does quadratus lumborum insert?
options: Posterior part of the iliac crest
Lower border of the 12th rib and transverse processes of L1–L4
Transverse process of L5 and iliolumbar ligament
questions.explanation: Quadratus lumborum arises from the posterior iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament and inserts into the 12th rib and upper lumbar transverse processes. It fixes the 12th rib in inspiration and, acting on one side, bends the trunk sideways. Psoas major arises from the vertebral bodies and inserts into the lesser trochanter.
notes: This is the muscle's origin.
This is the insertion of iliopsoas.
This is part of the muscle's origin.
This is the origin of psoas major.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Which muscles form the pelvic diaphragm?
options: External anal sphincter and deep transverse perineal muscle
questions.explanation: The pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) consists of the funnel-shaped levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus behind. Obturator internus and piriformis are in the lateral and posterior walls of the pelvis; bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus are superficial perineal muscles.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: The tendinous arch from which levator ani arises is a thickening of the fascia of which muscle?
questions.explanation: Levator ani arises in front from the back of the pubis, behind from the ischial spine, and in between from the tendinous arch of levator ani formed by a thickening of the obturator internus fascia. So the upper part of obturator internus lies within the pelvis and its lower part in the perineum (lateral wall of the ischio-anal fossa).

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: After a difficult vaginal delivery a patient with incontinence of flatus and faeces is found to have a tear of the anal sphincter complex. Which nerve supplies the voluntarily controlled external anal sphincter?
questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter is striated muscle supplied by the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve; a difficult delivery can cause both a muscle tear and stretch injury of the pudendal nerve. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle controlled by autonomic nerves (sympathetic: contraction).
notes: It supplies the cremaster and the skin of the upper front of the thigh.
It supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh.
They are parasympathetic; they relax the internal sphincter.
It is sympathetic; it contracts the internal sphincter.

questions.stem: Which rotator cuff muscles are supplied by the suprascapular nerve?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch to supply supraspinatus, then winds around the spinoglenoid notch to supply infraspinatus. Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve and subscapularis by the subscapular nerves; teres major is not part of the rotator cuff.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old with shoulder pain has the arm passively abducted to 90° and released; he cannot lower it slowly and it drops suddenly. What is the most likely tear?
questions.explanation: The drop-arm test indicates a supraspinatus tear; this tendon is the rotator cuff tendon most exposed to impingement and degeneration in the narrow space under the acromion. In subscapularis tears the lift-off and belly-press tests are abnormal; in teres minor tears external rotation strength is impaired.

questions.stem: Which structure passes through the triangular space (between teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps)?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
questions.explanation: The triangular space contains only the circumflex scapular artery, which joins the anastomotic network behind the scapula. The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery pass through the quadrangular space, the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery through the triangular interval between triceps and teres major.
notes: It accompanies latissimus dorsi; it does not pass through this space.
They pass through the quadrangular space.
It passes through the suprascapular notch.
They pass through the triangular interval below teres major.

questions.stem: Which structures pass through the triangular interval between the lower border of teres major and the long and lateral heads of triceps?
options: Ulnar nerve and superior ulnar collateral artery
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
questions.explanation: The radial nerve passes from the axilla to the back of the arm through this interval and reaches the radial groove of the humerus with the profunda brachii artery; it is injured here in fractures of the humeral shaft.

questions.stem: Where does deltoid insert?
options: Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus
questions.explanation: Deltoid arises from the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula and inserts into the deltoid tuberosity on the lateral surface of the humeral shaft. It is the main muscle of abduction of the arm between 15° and 90°; it is supplied by the axillary nerve.

questions.stem: Where does the short head of biceps brachii arise?
options: From the tip of the coracoid process
questions.explanation: The short head arises from the coracoid process by a common tendon with coracobrachialis; the long head arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and glenoid labrum, and its tendon runs through the joint capsule down into the intertubercular sulcus.
notes: This is the origin of the long head of triceps.
This is the origin of deltoid.
This is the origin of the long head.
This is the insertion of subscapularis.

questions.stem: Which statement about the bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus) is true?
options: It covers the brachial artery and median nerve in the cubital fossa
It is the tendon of brachialis
It forms the floor of the cubital fossa
It attaches to the radial tuberosity
questions.explanation: The aponeurosis passing medially from the biceps tendon blends with the deep fascia of the forearm; it covers the brachial artery and median nerve and lies beneath the median cubital vein. So in venous procedures it protects the structures beneath it.
notes: The radial nerve lies on the lateral side of the cubital fossa, between brachioradialis and brachialis.
It separates from biceps brachii.
The floor is formed by brachialis and supinator.
The biceps tendon attaches to the radial tuberosity.

questions.stem: Where does brachioradialis insert?
options: Middle of the lateral surface of the radial shaft
Base of the radial styloid process
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis arises from the lateral supracondylar ridge and inserts into the lower end of the radius. It flexes the elbow with the forearm half-pronated; it is an elbow flexor supplied by the radial nerve. Pronator teres inserts into the middle of the radial shaft.

questions.stem: From where do the superficial flexor muscles of the forearm arise by a common tendon?
questions.explanation: Pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor carpi ulnaris arise by the common flexor tendon from the medial epicondyle. Overloading this tendon causes medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow); the extensors arise from the lateral epicondyle.

questions.stem: Which quadrilateral muscle lies distally in the deepest layer of the anterior forearm?
questions.explanation: Pronator quadratus runs between the anterior surfaces of the distal quarters of the ulna and radius; it is the main muscle initiating pronation and holds the distal radio-ulnar joint together. It is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve.

questions.stem: Which nerve is compressed in the supinator canal (arcade of Frohse), and what is the typical finding?
options: Median nerve – thenar wasting and ape hand
Anterior interosseous nerve – inability to make the 'OK' sign
Posterior interosseous nerve – loss of finger extension with sensation preserved
Superficial branch of the radial nerve – sensory loss on the back of the hand only
questions.explanation: The deep branch of the radial nerve can be compressed as it passes between the two heads of supinator (arcade of Frohse). Because it is a motor branch, the fingers cannot be extended at the MCP joints, but there is no sensory loss. The branches to ECRL and brachioradialis arise higher, so wrist extension is preserved and deviates radially.

questions.stem: Where does the palmaris longus tendon pass at the wrist?
options: In front of the flexor retinaculum (outside the carpal tunnel)
questions.explanation: The palmaris longus tendon passes in front of the retinaculum and continues into the palmar aponeurosis; it is absent in 10–15% of people and is often used for tendon grafts. It is felt in the middle of the wrist, just in front of the median nerve.

questions.stem: Which tendons lie in the 1st extensor compartment on the dorsum of the wrist?
options: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
questions.explanation: The compartments beneath the extensor retinaculum, from radial to ulnar: 1) APL–EPB, 2) ECRL–ECRB, 3) EPL, 4) ED–EI, 5) EDM, 6) ECU. Tenosynovitis of the first compartment is De Quervain's disease.
notes: They are in the 4th compartment.
They are in the 2nd compartment.
It is in the 3rd compartment.
It is in the 6th compartment.

questions.stem: Which tendon changes direction around the dorsal tubercle of the radius (Lister's tubercle)?
questions.explanation: In the 3rd compartment the EPL tendon uses Lister's tubercle as a pulley to turn towards the thumb. After distal radius fractures, friction and impaired blood supply at this point can lead to delayed rupture.

questions.stem: Where do the lumbricals of the hand arise?
options: From the sides of the metacarpals
From the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus
From the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis
