questions.explanation: The lumbricals arise from the deep flexor tendons and attach to the radial border of the extensor expansion; they flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints. The 1st and 2nd lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve, the 3rd and 4th by the ulnar nerve. The interossei arise from the metacarpals.

questions.stem: Which bony structures bound Guyon's canal (ulnar canal)?
questions.explanation: Guyon's canal lies between the pisiform (medially) and the hook of the hamate (laterally), between the palmar carpal ligament and the flexor retinaculum; the ulnar nerve and ulnar artery pass through it. Compression is common in cyclists; because the dorsal cutaneous branch does not enter the canal, sensation on the back of the hand is preserved.

questions.stem: Which is the principal muscle producing opposition of the thumb?
questions.explanation: Opponens pollicis draws the 1st metacarpal forwards and medially and rotates it medially, bringing the pulp of the thumb against the other fingers. It is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve; injury to this branch abolishes opposition.

questions.stem: In a patient with a glass cut on the ulnar border of the hand, only the deep branch of the ulnar nerve is divided. Which of the following findings is NOT expected?
options: Sensory loss over the hypothenar region and little finger
Weakness in gripping paper between the fingers
questions.explanation: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve is purely motor: it supplies the hypothenar muscles, the interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, adductor pollicis and the deep head of FPB. Sensation of the hypothenar skin and little finger is carried by the superficial branch and is therefore preserved.

questions.stem: Where does gluteus maximus insert?
options: Anterior surface of the greater trochanter
Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
Medial lip of the linea aspera
questions.explanation: The superficial fibres of gluteus maximus insert into the iliotibial tract, its deep lower fibres into the gluteal tuberosity of the femur. It is a powerful extensor and lateral rotator of the hip; it is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve.
notes: This is the insertion of gluteus minimus.
This is the insertion of gluteus medius.
This is the insertion of the adductors.
This is the insertion of iliopsoas.

questions.stem: Which muscle inserts into the anterior surface of the greater trochanter?
questions.explanation: Gluteus minimus inserts into the anterior surface of the greater trochanter, medius into its lateral surface and piriformis into its upper border. Obturator externus attaches in the trochanteric fossa and quadratus femoris to the quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest.

questions.stem: Which lateral rotator of the hip has a tendon that passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: Obturator internus arises inside the pelvis; as its tendon leaves through the lesser sciatic foramen it turns at a right angle over the lesser sciatic notch and runs between the gemelli to the greater trochanter. Piriformis passes through the greater sciatic foramen; the others lie outside the pelvis.

questions.stem: A patient who sits for long periods on hard surfaces has pain radiating from the buttock down the back of the leg; it worsens with the hip in flexion, adduction and internal rotation, and lumbar MRI is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve usually passes below piriformis (sometimes through it); stretching or hypertrophy of the muscle can compress the nerve and cause sciatica that does not originate in the spine. The FAIR position (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) stretches the muscle and so increases the pain.

questions.stem: Which muscle covers the roof (anteromedial wall) of the adductor canal?
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of Hunter's canal is vastus medialis and its posterior wall adductor longus and magnus; the roof is formed by the vasto-adductor membrane with sartorius over it. The femoral artery and vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis pass through the canal.
notes: It forms the posterior wall of the canal.
It is not related to the canal.
It forms the lateral wall of the canal.
It forms the posterior wall of the canal.

questions.stem: Where does gracilis insert?
options: Into the medial condyle of the femur
Into the head of the fibula
Into the upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
questions.explanation: Gracilis is a long thin muscle on the medial side of the thigh arising from the inferior pubic ramus; with sartorius and semitendinosus it forms the pes anserinus. It adducts the hip and flexes the knee; it is supplied by the obturator nerve.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the lower oblique fibres of vastus medialis (VMO)?
options: Preventing lateral displacement of the patella
questions.explanation: The VMO fibres attach to the patella from the medial side at a nearly horizontal angle; by balancing the laterally pulling component of quadriceps they keep the patella in the trochlea. Weakness predisposes to patellofemoral pain and lateral patellar dislocation. The muscle that pulls the bursa upwards is articularis genus.

questions.stem: Which muscles form the superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa?
options: Plantaris and the lateral head of gastrocnemius
questions.explanation: The superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa is semimembranosus and semitendinosus, the superolateral boundary biceps femoris, and the inferior boundaries the medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius (plantaris accompanies the lateral head).
notes: They are at the inferolateral boundary.
They are the inferior boundaries.
It is the superolateral boundary.
They do not take part in the boundaries of the fossa.

questions.stem: What do the hamstring muscles have in common?
options: They arise from the ischial tuberosity and cross both the hip and knee joints
All are supplied by the femoral nerve
The short head of biceps femoris also fully meets these criteria
All insert into the head of the fibula
questions.explanation: The true hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, the long head of biceps femoris and the hamstring part of adductor magnus) arise from the ischial tuberosity, extend the hip and flex the knee, and are supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. The short head of biceps femoris arises from the linea aspera, crosses only the knee and is supplied by the fibular part.

questions.stem: What is the order of structures in the femoral triangle from lateral to medial?
options: Femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal
Femoral nerve, femoral vein, femoral artery, femoral canal
Femoral canal, femoral vein, femoral artery, femoral nerve
Femoral vein, femoral artery, femoral nerve, femoral canal
Femoral artery, femoral nerve, femoral vein, femoral canal
questions.explanation: From lateral to medial, 'NAVEL': nerve, artery, vein, empty space (femoral canal) and lymphatics. The femoral sheath encloses the artery, vein and canal; the nerve lies outside the sheath. A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal and lies medial to the vein.

questions.stem: After pelvic surgery a patient has sensory loss over the middle of the medial thigh, has difficulty crossing the legs, and swings the leg outwards when walking. Which nerve has been damaged?
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve runs on the lateral pelvic wall, close to the ovary and the pelvic lymph nodes; it leaves through the obturator canal and supplies the adductor muscles and part of the skin of the medial thigh. When it is damaged adduction is weak and the leg swings outwards during walking.
notes: It supplies gluteus medius and minimus; its injury causes a Trendelenburg gait.
It supplies the hamstrings and everything below the knee.
It carries only sensation from the lateral thigh.
It supplies quadriceps and the front of the thigh.

questions.stem: Which muscles insert into the iliotibial tract?
options: Tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus
questions.explanation: The iliotibial band is a thickening of the fascia lata on the lateral side of the thigh; above, TFL and the superficial fibres of gluteus maximus join it, and below it attaches to Gerdy's tubercle of the tibia. It stabilises the lateral side of the knee and the hip during standing.

questions.stem: Where is pain most often felt in iliotibial band friction syndrome?
options: Over the lateral epicondyle of the femur, on the lateral side of the knee
At the lower pole of the patella
questions.explanation: In runners, with the knee at 20–30° of flexion the band slides back and forth over the lateral epicondyle, and repeated friction causes pain on the lateral side of the knee. Pes anserinus bursitis causes pain medially, Osgood–Schlatter disease at the tibial tuberosity and jumper's knee at the lower pole of the patella.

questions.stem: What is the order of structures in the popliteal fossa from superficial to deep?
options: Popliteal vein – tibial nerve – popliteal artery
Popliteal artery – tibial nerve – popliteal vein
Tibial nerve – popliteal vein – popliteal artery
Tibial nerve – popliteal artery – popliteal vein
Popliteal artery – popliteal vein – tibial nerve
questions.explanation: In the popliteal fossa the tibial nerve is most superficial, the popliteal vein lies deep to it, and the popliteal artery is deepest and closest to the femur. That is why the artery is most at risk in supracondylar fractures of the femur.

questions.stem: Where does popliteus arise?
options: From the medial condyle of the femur
From the head of the fibula
From the soleal line of the tibia
From the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle (and the lateral meniscus)
From the lower pole of the patella
questions.explanation: The popliteus tendon passes inside the joint capsule to attach to the lateral femoral condyle; the muscle attaches to the posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line. It unlocks the knee from full extension by rotating the femur laterally, and pulls the lateral meniscus backwards so that it is not trapped.

questions.stem: Which muscle is the strongest invertor of the foot and dynamically supports the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.explanation: The tibialis posterior tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and fans out to the navicular tuberosity and the plantar surfaces of the other tarsal bones. Tendon dysfunction is the commonest cause of acquired flatfoot in adults; the patient cannot rise onto the toes on one foot.

questions.stem: Where does the fibularis longus tendon insert in the sole of the foot?
options: Into the medial cuneiform and the base of the 1st metatarsal
Into the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal
Into the base of the 2nd metatarsal
Into the lateral surface of the cuboid
questions.explanation: The fibularis longus tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, then through the plantar groove of the cuboid, crossing the sole to reach the medial side; it plantarflexes and everts the foot and supports the transverse arch. Fibularis brevis inserts into the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal.
notes: This is the main insertion of tibialis posterior.
This is the insertion of fibularis brevis.
This is not an insertion of this muscle.
The tendon passes through the groove under the cuboid; it does not attach there.

questions.stem: Which pair of tendons supports the foot from below like a 'stirrup'?
options: Tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus
Extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior from the medial side and fibularis longus from the lateral side both attach to the medial cuneiform and the base of the 1st metatarsal; together the two tendons form a stirrup under the foot that suspends the transverse and medial arches and balances inversion and eversion.

questions.stem: Which statement about soleus is true?
options: It crosses both the knee and ankle joints
It arises from the femoral condyles
It is the main plantarflexor of the ankle when the knee is flexed
It is supplied by the deep fibular nerve
questions.explanation: Soleus arises from the tibia and fibula and crosses only the ankle. When the knee is flexed, gastrocnemius is slack, so plantarflexion is produced mainly by soleus; as a postural muscle it works continuously during standing, and it is supplied by the tibial nerve.

questions.stem: A patient describes burning and numbness on the medial side of the heel and in the sole after long runs; percussion behind and below the medial malleolus produces paraesthesia. Which nerve is compressed?
questions.explanation: In tarsal tunnel syndrome the tibial nerve or its plantar branches are compressed beneath the flexor retinaculum between the medial malleolus and the calcaneus, causing sensory disturbance in the sole and weakness of the intrinsic muscles. In the anterior tarsal tunnel the deep fibular nerve is compressed.

questions.stem: Which structures are found in the second layer of the muscles of the sole?
options: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi
Quadratus plantae, the lumbricals and the FDL and FHL tendons
Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis and flexor digiti minimi brevis
The interossei and the fibularis longus and tibialis posterior tendons
questions.explanation: The four layers of the sole: 1) abductor hallucis, FDB, abductor digiti minimi; 2) quadratus plantae, the lumbricals, the FDL and FHL tendons; 3) FHB, adductor hallucis, FDMB; 4) the interossei with the fibularis longus and tibialis posterior tendons.
notes: This is the 1st layer.
These are two muscles from different layers.
This is the 3rd layer.
This is the 4th layer.

questions.stem: Through which toe does the axis of abduction–adduction of the toes pass?
questions.explanation: In the foot the dorsal interossei move the toes away from the axis of the 2nd toe and the plantar interossei bring them towards it. In the hand this axis is the 3rd finger.

questions.stem: Where do the short extensor muscles on the dorsum of the foot arise?
options: From the lower end of the fibula
From the bases of the metatarsals
From the neck of the talus
From the superolateral surface of the calcaneus (in front of the sinus tarsi)
questions.explanation: Extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis arise from the superolateral surface of the calcaneus; they are felt as a soft mass on the lateral side of the dorsum of the foot that can be mistaken for oedema or a lump. Both are supplied by the deep fibular nerve.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression?
questions.explanation: All muscles of facial expression develop from the 2nd pharyngeal arch and are supplied by the facial nerve. The muscles of mastication come from the 1st arch and are supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the muscles of mastication?
questions.explanation: Masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid develop from the 1st pharyngeal arch and are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.stem: Which muscle of mastication can be felt hardening in the cheek when the teeth are clenched?
questions.explanation: Masseter runs from the zygomatic arch to the outer surface of the mandibular ramus; it is one of the strongest jaw-closing muscles and is easily felt in the cheek when the teeth are clenched.

questions.stem: Which fan-shaped muscle of mastication lies in the temple region?
questions.explanation: Temporalis is the fan-shaped muscle filling the temporal fossa; its fibres converge on the coronoid process; it closes the jaw and its posterior fibres retract it.

questions.stem: Which muscle purses the lips (whistling, kissing)?
questions.explanation: Orbicularis oris is the sphincter muscle encircling the mouth; it closes and purses the lips. Buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth.

questions.stem: How many extraocular muscles move the eyeball?
questions.explanation: The eyeball is moved by four recti (superior, inferior, medial, lateral) and two obliques (superior, inferior). Levator palpebrae superioris raises the eyelid and does not move the eyeball.

questions.stem: Which prominent muscle on the side of the neck runs from behind the ear to the sternum and clavicle?
questions.explanation: Sternocleidomastoid runs from the mastoid process to the manubrium and medial clavicle; it is an important surface landmark dividing the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.

questions.stem: Which thin, broad muscle of facial expression covers the front of the neck under the skin?
questions.explanation: Platysma is a superficial muscle of facial expression running from the upper chest to the mandible and corner of the mouth; it is supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve.

questions.stem: Which superficial muscle of the upper back shrugs (elevates) the shoulders?
questions.explanation: The upper fibres of trapezius elevate the scapula (shrugging); the middle fibres retract it and the lower fibres depress it. Levator scapulae also helps elevation.

questions.stem: Which is the broadest muscle of the back?
questions.explanation: Latissimus dorsi is a broad triangular muscle covering the lower back and loin; it extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm (the climbing and swimming muscle).

questions.stem: Which muscle group runs along both sides of the spine and keeps the trunk upright?
questions.explanation: From lateral to medial, erector spinae consists of the iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns; it extends the spine and maintains upright posture.

questions.stem: Which is the most important (principal) muscle of respiration?
questions.explanation: In quiet breathing the diaphragm does most of the work of inspiration; when it contracts its dome descends and the vertical diameter of the thoracic cavity increases.

questions.stem: Which is the largest muscle on the front of the chest?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis major is the fan-shaped muscle covering the front of the chest; it adducts, medially rotates and flexes the arm.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Which muscle gives the 'six-pack' appearance of the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The tendinous intersections across rectus abdominis divide the muscle into segments and create its characteristic appearance.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Of the three flat muscles of the anterolateral abdominal wall, which is the most superficial?
questions.explanation: From superficial to deep: external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis. The fibres of the external oblique run like 'hands in pockets' (downwards and forwards).

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Between which two points does the inguinal ligament run?
options: Anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle
Anterior inferior iliac spine and ischial tuberosity
questions.explanation: The inguinal ligament is the rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis; it runs from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle and is an important landmark of the groin.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Where does the linea alba run?
options: Along the lateral border of rectus
Between the ASIS and pubic tubercle
From the umbilicus to the costal margin
Between the xiphoid process and the pubic symphysis
questions.explanation: The linea alba is the fibrous band between the two recti formed by the midline fusion of the aponeuroses of the abdominal muscles; the umbilicus lies on it.

questions.stem: Which triangular muscle gives the shoulder its rounded contour?
questions.explanation: Deltoid arises from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula and inserts on the deltoid tuberosity; it gives the shoulder its rounded contour and abducts the arm.

questions.stem: Which muscles form the rotator cuff?
options: Deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis
Supraspinatus, teres major, teres minor and latissimus dorsi
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres major and subscapularis
Subscapularis, pectoralis minor, teres minor and deltoid
questions.explanation: The rotator cuff (SITS) is the dynamic stabiliser holding the humeral head in the glenoid. Teres major is not part of the rotator cuff.

questions.stem: Which is the 'biceps' muscle on the front of the arm?
questions.explanation: Biceps brachii is the two-headed muscle on the front of the arm; it flexes the elbow and is a powerful supinator of the forearm.

questions.stem: Which is the main muscle that extends the elbow?
questions.explanation: Triceps brachii is the three-headed muscle on the back of the arm; it inserts on the olecranon and extends the elbow, assisted by anconeus.

questions.stem: In general, what movement do the muscles of the anterior (flexor) compartment of the forearm produce?
options: They flex the wrist and fingers
They extend the wrist and fingers
questions.explanation: The anterior forearm compartment contains the wrist and finger flexors and the pronators; most arise from the medial epicondyle and are supplied by the median nerve. The posterior compartment contains the extensors.

questions.stem: What is the muscular bulge at the base of the thumb called?
questions.explanation: The thenar eminence is formed by abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis; the bulge at the base of the little finger is the hypothenar eminence.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies most of the small (intrinsic) muscles of the hand?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles, interossei, 3rd–4th lumbricals, adductor pollicis and the deep head of FPB. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles and the 1st–2nd lumbricals.

questions.stem: Which is the largest and most superficial muscle of the gluteal region?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus is the most superficial and largest muscle of the buttock; it is the strongest extensor of the hip and is used in rising from sitting and climbing stairs.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest flexor of the hip?
questions.explanation: Iliopsoas (psoas major and iliacus) inserts on the lesser trochanter and is the strongest flexor of the hip.

questions.stem: Which hip abductor keeps the pelvis level when standing on one leg during walking?
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius (and minimus) abducts the hip on the stance side and prevents the opposite side of the pelvis from dropping. Its paralysis produces a positive Trendelenburg sign.

questions.stem: Which four-headed muscle on the front of the thigh extends the knee?
questions.explanation: Quadriceps femoris consists of rectus femoris and the three vasti; its common tendon encloses the patella and, via the patellar ligament, inserts on the tibial tuberosity to extend the knee.

questions.stem: What movement do the hamstring muscles on the back of the thigh produce at the knee?
questions.explanation: The hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) extend the hip and flex the knee.

questions.stem: What is the common function of the muscles of the medial compartment of the thigh?
options: Moving the thigh away from the midline (abduction)
Bringing the thigh towards the midline (adduction)
questions.explanation: The medial compartment muscles – adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis and pectineus – adduct the thigh; most are supplied by the obturator nerve.

questions.stem: Which muscle group forms the calf and inserts on the heel via the Achilles tendon?
questions.explanation: The two heads of gastrocnemius and soleus insert on the calcaneal tuberosity through the common Achilles tendon; they are the strongest plantar flexors of the ankle (rising on tiptoe).

questions.stem: Which muscles are found in the lateral compartment of the leg?
options: Tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus
Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
questions.explanation: The lateral compartment contains fibularis longus and brevis; they evert the foot and are supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.

questions.stem: What type of muscle tissue are skeletal muscles made of?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscles are cross-striated and voluntary, not involuntary; they are supplied by somatic motor nerves. Smooth muscle is found in the walls of internal organs, cardiac muscle in the heart.

questions.stem: Which is the smallest skeletal muscle of the body?
questions.explanation: Stapedius is a muscle of about 1 mm in the middle ear attached to the stapes; it damps stapes movement in loud sound, protecting the inner ear, and is supplied by the facial nerve.

questions.stem: What is the bony attachment of a muscle that stays fixed during movement called?
questions.explanation: The origin is usually the proximal, fixed attachment; the insertion is the attachment on the bone that moves. When a muscle contracts, the insertion approaches the origin.

questions.stem: Where does temporalis arise?
options: From the temporal fossa and temporal fascia
questions.explanation: Temporalis arises from the floor of the temporal fossa and the fascia covering it; it passes deep to the zygomatic arch to insert on the coronoid process.

questions.stem: What is the main function of buccinator?
options: Pressing the cheek against the teeth to keep food between them during chewing, and blowing
Raising the corner of the mouth
questions.explanation: Buccinator is the muscular layer of the cheek; it stops food escaping between cheek and teeth and tightens the cheek when blowing (playing the trumpet). It is supplied by the facial nerve and pierced by the parotid duct.

questions.stem: Which muscle pulls the corner of the mouth down (sad expression)?
questions.explanation: Depressor anguli oris runs from the lower border of the mandible to the corner of the mouth and pulls it down. Zygomaticus major pulls the corner upwards and outwards (smiling).

questions.stem: Which muscle divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles?
questions.explanation: The anterior triangle lies in front of SCM, the posterior triangle between SCM and trapezius. Omohyoid and digastric subdivide these triangles into smaller ones.

questions.stem: Where does scalenus anterior arise?
options: From the posterior tubercles of the C1–C4 transverse processes
From the anterior tubercles of the C3–C6 transverse processes
questions.explanation: Scalenus anterior arises from the anterior tubercles of the C3–C6 transverse processes and inserts on the scalene tubercle of the 1st rib; the phrenic nerve descends on its front.

questions.stem: Which fibres of trapezius retract the scapula (towards the spine)?
options: None; trapezius does not retract the scapula
questions.explanation: The middle fibres of trapezius retract the scapula. The upper fibres elevate it, the lower fibres depress it; upper and lower fibres together rotate it upwards.

questions.stem: What happens in the thoracic cavity when the diaphragm contracts?
options: The anteroposterior diameter of the chest decreases.
The ribs are pulled down and expiration occurs.
The dome rises and thoracic volume decreases.
The dome descends and the vertical diameter of the chest increases.
questions.explanation: When the diaphragm contracts its dome flattens and descends; the vertical diameter of the thoracic cavity increases and air flows in. Meanwhile intra-abdominal pressure rises.

questions.stem: What is the main action of serratus anterior?
options: Pulling the scapula forwards (protraction) and rotating it upwards
Depressing and pushing the scapula back
questions.explanation: Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the chest wall, pulls it forwards (the 'boxer's muscle') and, with trapezius, rotates it upwards so the arm can be raised above 90°.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies subclavius?
questions.explanation: The nerve to subclavius is a small branch of the upper trunk of the brachial plexus; it sometimes gives an accessory phrenic nerve that joins the phrenic nerve.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: What is the main function of transversus abdominis?
options: Compressing the abdominal wall to raise intra-abdominal pressure
questions.explanation: With its horizontal fibres transversus abdominis tightens the abdominal wall like a belt; it raises intra-abdominal pressure in coughing, straining, childbirth and forced expiration, and stabilises the trunk.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Which is the main structure forming the anterior wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The anterior wall of the inguinal canal is the external oblique aponeurosis (reinforced laterally by internal oblique fibres), the posterior wall the transversalis fascia (medially the conjoint tendon), and the floor the inguinal ligament.

questions.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a part of levator ani?
questions.explanation: Levator ani consists of puborectalis, pubococcygeus (with pubovaginalis/puboprostaticus fibres) and iliococcygeus. Coccygeus is a separate muscle of the pelvic diaphragm.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies teres minor?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor. Supraspinatus and infraspinatus are supplied by the suprascapular nerve, subscapularis and teres major by the subscapular nerves.

questions.stem: What is the innervation of brachialis?
options: Mainly the musculocutaneous nerve (its lateral part also receives radial fibres)
questions.explanation: The three muscles of the anterior arm compartment (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis) are supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve; the lateral part of brachialis additionally receives fibres from the radial nerve.

questions.stem: What are the function and innervation of anconeus?
questions.explanation: Anconeus is a small muscle running from the lateral epicondyle to the lateral surface of the olecranon; it assists triceps and tenses the elbow joint capsule.

questions.stem: What is the order of the superficial forearm flexors from lateral (radial) to medial (ulnar)?
options: Flexor carpi radialis, pronator teres, flexor carpi ulnaris, palmaris longus
Pronator teres, palmaris longus, flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris
Pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor carpi ulnaris
Palmaris longus, flexor carpi radialis, pronator teres, flexor carpi ulnaris
Flexor carpi ulnaris, palmaris longus, flexor carpi radialis, pronator teres
questions.explanation: Placing the right hand on the chest with the thumb lateral, you can count the four muscles: PT, FCR, PL, FCU. All arise from the common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle; FDS lies deep to them.

questions.stem: Where do the FDS and FDP tendons insert in the fingers?
options: FDS on the middle phalanx, FDP on the distal phalanx
FDS on the distal phalanx, FDP on the middle phalanx
FDS on the metacarpal head, FDP on the middle phalanx
questions.explanation: The FDS tendon splits in two at the level of the proximal phalanx (Camper's chiasm), and the FDP tendon passes through the split to reach the distal phalanx. DIP flexion is therefore produced only by FDP.

questions.stem: Which muscle allows the index finger to be extended independently of the other fingers?
questions.explanation: Extensor indicis is one of the deep forearm extensors and allows independent extension of the index finger (pointing). Its tendon is often used in tendon transfers.

questions.stem: Mallet finger is an injury of which structure?
options: Collateral ligament of the MCP joint
Volar plate of the PIP joint
Terminal part of the extensor tendon inserting on the distal phalanx
Central slip of the extensor tendon
Insertion of the FDP tendon on the distal phalanx
questions.explanation: A blow to the fingertip ruptures the end of the extensor tendon on the distal phalanx, and the patient cannot actively extend the DIP joint. A central slip injury causes a boutonnière deformity.

questions.stem: What is the main action of piriformis?
questions.explanation: Piriformis arises from the anterior surface of the sacrum, passes through the greater sciatic foramen and inserts on the greater trochanter; it laterally rotates the hip and abducts it when flexed.

questions.stem: What is the order of the deep lateral rotators of the hip from superior to inferior?
options: Obturator internus, piriformis, quadratus femoris, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior
Piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris
Quadratus femoris, gemellus inferior, obturator internus, gemellus superior, piriformis
Gemellus superior, piriformis, gemellus inferior, obturator internus, quadratus femoris
Piriformis, gemellus superior, obturator internus, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris
questions.explanation: With gluteus maximus removed, from top to bottom one sees piriformis, gemellus superior, the obturator internus tendon, gemellus inferior and quadratus femoris; obturator externus lies deeper.

questions.stem: What are the actions of sartorius?
options: Adducts and medially rotates the hip
Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip; flexes the knee
Extends the hip and extends the knee
questions.explanation: Sartorius performs all the movements of sitting cross-legged: hip flexion, abduction and lateral rotation, and knee flexion. It is supplied by the femoral nerve.

questions.stem: Which muscle forms the medial border of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded above by the inguinal ligament, laterally by sartorius and medially by the medial border of adductor longus. Its floor is formed by iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus.

questions.stem: Which spinal segment does the patellar (knee) reflex mainly test?
questions.explanation: The patellar reflex runs through the femoral nerve and segments L2–L4, especially L4. The Achilles reflex tests S1, the biceps reflex C5 and the triceps reflex C7.

questions.stem: Which spinal segment does the biceps tendon reflex mainly test?
questions.explanation: The biceps reflex runs through the musculocutaneous nerve and tests C5–C6, especially C5. The brachioradialis reflex is for C6, the triceps reflex for C7.

questions.stem: Which of the following muscles is NOT in the anterior compartment of the leg?
questions.explanation: The anterior compartment contains tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL and fibularis tertius, supplied by the deep fibular nerve. Fibularis brevis is in the lateral compartment (superficial fibular nerve).

questions.stem: Where do the two heads of gastrocnemius arise?
options: From the posterior surfaces of the tibia and fibula
From the posterior surfaces of the medial and lateral femoral condyles
From the patella and patellar ligament
questions.explanation: Because gastrocnemius arises from the femoral condyles it also crosses the knee and helps flex it. Soleus arises from the tibia and fibula and does not cross the knee.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies popliteus?
questions.explanation: Popliteus is the muscle in the floor of the popliteal fossa; it unlocks the knee from full extension and is supplied by the tibial nerve.

questions.stem: Which muscles are in the first (most superficial) layer of the sole of the foot?
options: Extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis
Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi
Flexor hallucis brevis and adductor hallucis
questions.explanation: The plantar muscles form four layers: 1. abductor hallucis, FDB, abductor digiti minimi; 2. quadratus plantae, lumbricals; 3. FHB, adductor hallucis, FDMB; 4. interossei.

questions.stem: A basketball player landing from a jump reports pain at the front of the knee and cannot actively extend it; the patella lies higher than normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: When the patellar ligament ruptures, quadriceps pulls the patella upwards (patella alta) and, with the extensor mechanism disrupted, the knee cannot be actively extended. In a quadriceps tendon rupture the patella stays low (patella baja).

questions.stem: Which is the only palatal muscle supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3)?
questions.explanation: All palatal muscles are supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus; the only exception is tensor veli palatini, derived from the 1st arch (V3). Tensor tympani is likewise supplied by V3.

questions.stem: Which option gives the innervation of the middle ear muscles correctly?
options: Tensor tympani – mandibular nerve (V3); stapedius – facial nerve (VII)
questions.explanation: Tensor tympani derives from the 1st arch (V3), stapedius from the 2nd arch (VII). Facial nerve lesions proximal to the nerve to stapedius cause hyperacusis.

questions.stem: From which vertebrae does the right crus of the diaphragm arise?
questions.explanation: The right crus arises from the bodies of L1–L3, the shorter left crus from L1–L2. Fibres of the right crus encircle the oesophagus like a sling to form the oesophageal hiatus.

questions.stem: What are the most common type and site of congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
options: Morgagni hernia – anteromedial, mostly on the right
Bochdalek hernia – anteromedial, mostly on the right
Bochdalek hernia – posterolateral, mostly on the left
Morgagni hernia – posterolateral, on the left
questions.explanation: A Bochdalek hernia forms posterolaterally (most often on the left) when the pleuroperitoneal membrane fails to close, causing lung hypoplasia in the newborn. A Morgagni hernia is rarer and anteromedial.

questions.stem: What is the typical arm position in Erb–Duchenne palsy (upper trunk, C5–C6)?
options: Arm normal, only thumb opposition lost
Arm adducted and medially rotated, forearm extended and pronated ('waiter's tip')
Arm abducted and laterally rotated, forearm flexed
questions.explanation: In C5–C6 injury deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis are paralysed; the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated, the forearm extended and pronated. It results from birth trauma and forced widening of the shoulder–neck angle.

questions.stem: Which muscles are most affected in Klumpke palsy (lower trunk, C8–T1)?
questions.explanation: Injury of the C8–T1 roots (traction of the arm in excessive abduction) affects all intrinsic hand muscles and produces a claw hand; if T1 sympathetic fibres are involved, Horner syndrome may accompany it.

questions.stem: When the radial nerve is injured in a fracture of the middle third of the humerus, why is triceps brachii usually spared?
options: The branches to triceps leave before the nerve enters the spiral groove.
Triceps is supplied by the axillary nerve.
Triceps is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
The nerve does not pass through triceps in the spiral groove.
questions.explanation: In the upper arm, before entering the radial groove, the radial nerve gives its branches to the long and medial heads of triceps. In a mid-shaft fracture elbow extension is therefore mostly preserved, while wrist drop develops.

questions.stem: A rugby player whose finger was forcibly extended while grabbing an opponent's jersey cannot actively flex the DIP joint (jersey finger). Which tendon has ruptured?
options: Terminal part of the extensor tendon
questions.explanation: In jersey finger the FDP tendon avulses from the base of the distal phalanx; the ring finger is most often affected. Because only FDP flexes the DIP joint, this movement is lost.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies quadratus femoris?
options: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
questions.explanation: Quadratus femoris and gemellus inferior are supplied by the nerve to quadratus femoris from the sacral plexus. Obturator internus and gemellus superior are supplied by the nerve to obturator internus.

questions.stem: Which muscles form the floor of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: From lateral to medial the floor of the femoral triangle is formed by iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus; its roof is the fascia lata and cribriform fascia.

questions.stem: Which hamstring muscle tears most often in sprinters?
questions.explanation: The long head of biceps femoris is the most frequently injured hamstring because it is overstretched eccentrically at the end of the swing phase of running.

questions.stem: What is the function of quadratus plantae?
options: Correcting the oblique pull of the FDL tendon so the toes flex straight
questions.explanation: Quadratus plantae runs from the calcaneus to the lateral border of the FDL tendon; it corrects FDL's oblique pull from behind the medial malleolus so that the toes flex straight. It is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.

questions.stem: After total hip replacement a patient cannot lift the foot (foot drop) and has numbness on the outer side of the leg. What is the most likely damage?
options: Injury of the fibular division of the sciatic nerve
questions.explanation: In hip surgery the fibular division of the sciatic nerve, more superficial and protected by less connective tissue, is injured more often; dorsiflexion and eversion are lost, with sensory loss on the outer leg.
